What we do

Three specialties. One standard of work.

We keep our focus narrow on purpose — the three kinds of residential work San Francisco homeowners ask for most, done properly.

01 — REMODELS

Remodels that respect the house

Open up a compartmentalized Edwardian floor plan, redo a kitchen that finally works for how you cook, or take a whole home down to the studs — while keeping the character that made you buy it.

  • Kitchen & bathroom remodels
  • Whole-home & gut renovations
  • Additions & floor-plan rework
  • Seismic retrofit & structural repair
02 — ADUs

ADUs for family, guests & income

Accessory dwelling units are the smartest square footage in San Francisco. We design and build units that fit your lot, your budget, and California's streamlined ADU rules.

  • Detached backyard cottages
  • Garage & basement conversions
  • Junior ADUs (JADUs)
  • Feasibility, plans & permit support
03 — NEW HOMES

New homes, from the ground up

Ground-up custom homes on infill and hillside lots — foundation to finishes. We build for San Francisco's slopes, soils, and sightlines, and coordinate with your architect throughout.

  • Custom single-family homes
  • Hillside & steep-lot construction
  • Teardown & rebuild projects
  • Design-build coordination
What we build

The kind of work we take on

San Francisco homes ask a lot of a builder — light, views, slope, and a century of earlier decisions behind the walls. This is the work we're set up for.

Built for San Francisco

Local knowledge is a building material.

Every city rewards builders who know it. San Francisco demands it — its housing stock, its hills, and its permit process all have their own rules.

1

Victorians & Edwardians

Old-growth framing, lath and plaster, unreinforced foundations, and a hundred years of layered remodels. We open walls expecting surprises — and budget for them honestly.

2

Hills, soils & seismic

Steep lots, Bay mud, and earthquake country. Retaining, drainage, and seismic work are planned with engineers from day one, not discovered mid-project.

3

Permits without the runaround

We prepare complete submittals for the SF Department of Building Inspection, track reviews, and keep you posted on where things stand — including what's realistic on timing.

4

Tight lots, close neighbors

Zero-lot-line work, shared walls, and narrow streets. Clean sites, protected finishes, and neighbors who get a heads-up before loud days.

ADU spotlight

Four ways to add a second home to your lot

Not sure which ADU fits your property? Start here — then tell us about your lot in the project brief and we'll talk through feasibility.

Backyard cottage

A detached unit in the rear yard — the most private option, and often the best for long-term rental or extended family.

Garage conversion

Turn an underused garage into a studio or one-bedroom. The structure already exists, which can shorten the build.

Basement / lower-level unit

San Francisco's raised homes often hide a full floor of potential. We handle headroom, light, egress, and moisture properly.

Junior ADU (JADU)

A compact unit carved from within the existing home — up to 500 sq ft under California law, with a simpler approval path.

Good to know: California law has streamlined ADU permitting in recent years, and San Francisco runs its own ADU program — many projects that once stalled now move. Every lot is different, though: setbacks, height, and utilities decide what's possible, which is why we start with feasibility before drawings.

How it works

A clear path from idea to keys

No mystery pricing, no disappearing contractor. Here's what working with J Farley Construction looks like, step by step.

01

Walkthrough & conversation

We visit your home or lot, listen to what you want, and talk honestly about what's possible, what it involves, and what drives cost.

02

Scope, design & permits

You get a written scope and budget range. We coordinate plans with your architect or designer and submit for permits with SF DBI.

03

Build, with updates

Work starts on an agreed schedule. You get regular progress updates and a single point of contact for every question, change, and decision.

04

Final walkthrough

We walk the finished work together, close out inspections, and don't call it done until the punch list is done too.

Common questions

Before you break ground

Almost always, yes. Structural changes, additions, ADUs, and most kitchen and bath work that moves plumbing or electrical need permits from the SF Department of Building Inspection. Cosmetic work like painting usually doesn't. We confirm what's required for your scope and handle the submittal as part of the project.

It depends on scope and permitting. A single bathroom is a matter of weeks once permits are in hand; a whole-home remodel or ADU runs to months; a new home is a longer build again. Permitting in San Francisco is often the longest single phase, so we give you a schedule that separates permit time from construction time — and we update it as things move.

Often, yes — for kitchen, bath, or partial remodels we can phase work, seal off construction areas, and keep a working bathroom. For gut renovations and structural work, moving out for a stretch is usually safer and faster. We'll tell you honestly which camp your project falls into before you sign anything.

Gladly — most of our larger projects are architect-led, and we prefer to be involved early so pricing and buildability shape the design, not surprise it. If you don't have an architect yet, we can point you toward local designers and architects who fit your project type.

After a walkthrough, you get a written scope with a budget range. Once plans are developed, that becomes a detailed proposal before construction starts. Changes during the build are priced and approved in writing before the work happens — no surprise line items at the end.

Most single-family lots in San Francisco can fit some form of ADU — detached, conversion, or junior. The deciding factors are rear-yard space, setbacks, height limits, and utility capacity. Tell us your address and what you're imagining in the project brief, and we'll assess feasibility as the first step.
